questions.question: Describe how you would find where a bar magnet is strongest and how you would make the test fair, and explain why a free-swinging magnet points north.
questions.expected_answer: Scatter paper clips near the magnet and count how many hang in a chain from each end and from the middle; the chains form at the ends, the poles, where the force is concentrated, and the middle holds almost none. To make the test fair, use the same clips, the same chaining method and the same pole for each magnet and repeat each count three times, recording results in a table. A magnet hung on a thread settles north and south because the Earth is itself a huge magnet; the end pointing north is the north-seeking pole, marked N, and a compass is a small magnet doing the same.

questions.question: State the law of magnets, explain why repulsion is the only proof that an object is a magnet, and describe what happens when a bar magnet is cut in half.
questions.expected_answer: Unlike poles attract and like poles repel. Plain iron is attracted to both poles of a magnet and never pushes back, so attraction cannot distinguish a magnet from iron; only repulsion, which happens when two like poles meet, proves that both objects are magnets. The force acts across a gap and through non-magnetic materials, so magnetism is a non-contact force. Cutting a magnet in half does not separate the poles; each half becomes a complete magnet with its own north and south pole, because poles always come in pairs.

questions.question: Explain how iron filings and a plotting compass reveal a magnetic field, how field lines are drawn, and how the pattern differs between attracting and repelling poles.
questions.expected_answer: Filings sprinkled on paper over a magnet line up along curved field lines that run from pole to pole, crowded at the poles where the field is strong and sparse at the sides where it is weak. A plotting compass maps a line by marking where its needle points, moving to that dot and repeating until the trail reaches the other pole; lines are drawn from N to S outside the magnet. With unlike poles facing, the lines run straight across the gap and join the magnets, showing attraction; with like poles facing, the lines bend away from each other and leave an empty region between the poles, showing repulsion.
